points.t: Eczema that **matches an exposure** in time and place: wet-work hands, under a watch, eyelids from nail varnish.
**Irritant**: direct barrier injury. **Allergic**: type IV reaction 24–72 h after re-exposure.
Avoid the cause, soap substitute + emollient, topical steroid matched to site.
Occupational hand dermatitis, airborne allergy on the face, allergy to the treatment itself.

cause.lead: Two routes to the same eczema.
points: **Irritant (ICD)**: water, detergents, solvents, friction. No sensitisation; dose matters.
**Allergic (ACD)**: nickel, fragrance, rubber accelerators, MI/MCI preservatives, PPD hair dye, topical medicines.
ACD needs prior **sensitisation**; then tiny amounts trigger it.
Mixed ICD + ACD is common on hands; about **four-fifths** of occupational hand dermatitis starts as irritant.

visuals.caption: Irritant (left): water and detergent crack the surface barrier directly. Allergic (right): allergen particles are captured by Langerhans cells and a delayed T-cell response floods the upper skin, with small fluid pockets (spongiosis).
visuals.alt: Two skin sections comparing irritant and allergic contact dermatitis

features.lead: Both look eczematous; the pattern gives the clue.
points: **ICD**: burning or stinging > itch; sharp borders early; finger webs in wet work.
**ACD**: itch dominates; **geometric** shapes (glove, plaster, jewellery); may spread beyond contact.
**Face**: eyelids and hairline (cosmetics, hair dye); airborne fragrance on exposed skin.
**Tattoo**: eczema or lichenoid reaction in one ink colour.
**Skin of colour**: less redness; more violaceous pigment and lichenification.

visuals.caption: Classic allergic contact sites: eyelids (nail varnish, cosmetics), earlobes (nickel), wrist (watch strap), below the navel (jeans stud), hands (gloves, products).
visuals.alt: Body map of typical allergic contact dermatitis sites

points: Job, hobbies, cosmetics, topical medicines.
**Better on holiday?**
Clinical: an exposure story.
No confirmatory test.
Refer if **chronic, recurrent, occupational, facial or resistant**.
Baseline series ± own products; photopatch if sunscreen suspected.
Prick / IgE tests are for **immediate contact urticaria** (e.g. latex), not ACD.

cards.name: Atopic eczema
cards.clue: Flexural history; not limited to a contact site.

cards.name: Tinea
cards.clue: Annular scaly edge; scrape for mycology.

manage.lead: Remove the cause. Improvement can take weeks.

points: Identify and **avoid** the irritant or allergen.
Soap substitute + liberal emollient.
Cotton liners under gloves for wet work.
**Short topical corticosteroid** matched to site and severity.
Face and flexures: mild to moderate potency.
Refer for **patch testing** when indicated (CKS / BAD / PCDS).
Fit note and workplace adjustments.
RIDDOR reporting is employer-led: recognise and signpost.

limits.t: Fire risk on fabrics; slippery floors.
Grey-brown pigment from cosmetics in darker skin: see contact & lichenoid pigmentation.

items.t: Severe **facial or eyelid swelling**, or systemic contact dermatitis.
**Occupational** disease threatening livelihood: early patch testing and workplace advice.
Suspected **airborne** allergy continuing despite stopping perfume.
Not healing on treatment: think allergy to the **medicament** itself.

pearls.t: Many hand “allergies” are **irritant**: treat the barrier hard anyway.
Atopic patients get ICD more easily and can still develop ACD.
PPD hair dye and nail-varnish eyelid patterns are classic teaching cases.
Check BNF / SmPC for topical steroid site limits.

quiz.q: Irritant or allergic: which needs prior sensitisation?
quiz.a: Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV). Irritant needs no sensitisation and is dose-dependent.

quiz.q: When does allergic contact dermatitis appear after re-exposure?
Which test confirms allergic contact dermatitis?
quiz.a: Patch testing (prick tests / IgE are for immediate contact urticaria).

quiz.q: Who should be referred for patch testing?
quiz.a: Chronic, recurrent, occupational, facial or treatment-resistant suspected allergic contact dermatitis.

quiz.q: A rash worsens under a cream you prescribed. Think?
quiz.a: Contact allergy to the medicament itself (e.g. topical antibiotic or steroid).
